The basic difference in limiting the project to the redevelopment area would be restricting the ability of the neighboring area in the removal of blighting influences. Many "borderline" areas would become breeding areas of blight. Total eradication of blighting influences could not be attained. The project area would be ringed with new blighting influences not under control of the program. The project area, tightly defined by natural and man made borders, if limited to less than those borders, would fail to achieve the objectives of the project, namely renewal and preservation of an entire neighborhood.
Renewal and preservation of the neighborhood have been the goals for the Randolph Communtiy. The character and intensity of future development has concerned the community from the outset. During the PAC group discussions on high rise apartments and elderly housing, the community examined the possible, alternative levels of intensity for the redevelopment plans and the respective impact each would have on neighborhood character and life styles. It was resolved that the existing character of two story housing, pedestrian orientation, and a variety of small scale recreation areas would be the most desirable and effective method of redevelopment.
3. The Location of the Project could be moved:
The project could be reassigned to another area. Other areas within the city of Richmond could qualify for rehabilitation and redevelopment programs. Relocation of the project would defeat any attempts to eliminate the blight and blighting influences in Randolph. The blighted area within Randolph would gradually expand and spread into the more stable sections. Bounded by distinct borders it is safe to assume that the deterioration would encompass all 380 acres and affect 12,000 inhabitants of the Randolph area. Other impacts would be a gradual collapse of citizen participation throughout the city. Citizen participation has not been stronger or more widely acclaimed than in the Randolph Area. The Randolph PAC has (and is) working with other PAC groups in the Fulton Project, Washington Park Project, and has contacted PAC groups in Portsmouth and Hampton, Virginia. It seems likely that the termination of the project would cause a credibility gap between these PAC groups and the Redevelopment Authority and HUD. In brief, relocation of the project would result in physical and social deterioration, causing perhaps irresponsible change to citizen-governmental relations.
